notes.h: What contaminants are and how they enter food
notes.b: A contaminant is an unwanted substance that gets into food by accident, at any stage from farm to plate.
points: Contaminants can enter during primary production on the farm, during processing, during packaging, during storage and during cooking.
A residue is a small amount of a substance left in food after it was used legitimately, such as a pesticide or a veterinary medicine.
General food law, set out in Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, requires that food placed on the market is not unsafe.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland coordinates national enforcement of food safety, including control of contaminants.
Pesticides are chemicals used on crops: insecticides against insects, fungicides against fungi and herbicides against weeds.
A withdrawal period is the minimum time between the last spraying and harvest, allowing residues to fall to a safe level.
Residues can remain on fruit, vegetables and cereals and so enter the diet.
Washing and peeling reduce the amount of pesticide residue on fresh produce.
Residues are monitored by official testing carried out by agencies under FSAI service contracts, including the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine and the HSE Public Analyst Laboratories.
Antibiotics are given to livestock to treat or prevent disease.
If milk or meat is sold before the withdrawal period has passed, antibiotic residues remain in the food.
Antibiotic residues in milk can prevent the lactic acid bacteria used for yoghurt and cheese from fermenting, so the product fails to set or ripen properly.
Antibiotic residues can cause allergic reactions in sensitive people and may contribute to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
Heavy metals such as lead, cadmium and mercury enter food from soil, water and air contaminated by industry or traffic.
Plants grown in contaminated soil can absorb metals, and shellfish filtering polluted water can accumulate them.
Mercury accumulates in large predatory fish such as shark and swordfish, a process known as bioaccumulation.
Because metals build up in the body over time, repeated exposure is a greater concern than a single exposure.

notes.h: Chemical contaminants from processing and packaging
points: Cleaning agents, lubricants and sanitisers used in food premises can contaminate food if they are not rinsed off or are misused.
Chemicals can migrate from packaging or other food-contact materials into food, particularly fatty or acidic foods.
Food-grade materials and separate storage of chemicals from food reduce the risk of contamination.
Pest control chemicals stored near food can contaminate it if the storage is not properly separated.
On the farm, good agricultural practice and observance of withdrawal periods control pesticide and veterinary residues.
Food businesses buy raw materials from approved suppliers and test them on reception.
Traceability records, including lot codes, allow a contaminated batch to be identified and recalled quickly.
Official control agencies sample and test food and raw materials to check that the limits on contaminants are met.

keyTerms.definition: An unwanted substance that enters food accidentally at any stage from production to consumption.
A small amount of a substance, such as a pesticide or veterinary medicine, that remains in food after legitimate use.
A chemical used to kill or control pests on crops, including insecticides, fungicides and herbicides.
The minimum time that must pass after a chemical is applied or administered before the crop, milk or meat can be sold.
A metal such as lead, cadmium or mercury that is toxic at low levels and can accumulate in the body.
The build-up of a substance in an organism over time, so that concentrations are higher in animals further up the food chain.
The transfer of chemicals from packaging or food-contact materials into the food they contain.
The ability to follow a food or ingredient through each stage of production and distribution using records such as lot codes.
The withdrawal of a food batch from sale and consumers when it is found to be unsafe.

questions.prompt: Name two sources of contamination in the food chain and explain how each one enters food.
questions.model: Pesticides: chemicals sprayed on crops to control insects, fungi or weeds leave residues on fruit, vegetables and cereals, which enter the diet if not removed by washing or peeling. Heavy metals: lead, cadmium or mercury present in soil, water or air contaminated by industry or traffic are absorbed by plants or accumulated by shellfish and predatory fish. Other valid sources: antibiotic residues in milk or meat sold before the withdrawal period has passed; chemicals migrating from packaging into the food.

questions.prompt: Discuss how contaminants can enter food at different stages of the food chain, and explain how a food business can control them.
questions.model: Primary production: pesticides applied to crops and veterinary medicines given to livestock leave residues if withdrawal periods are not observed; heavy metals from polluted soil and water are absorbed by plants and animals. Processing: cleaning agents, lubricants and sanitisers can contaminate food if they are misused or not rinsed off. Packaging and storage: chemicals can migrate from packaging into fatty or acidic foods, and pest control chemicals stored near food can contaminate it. Cooking: contaminants already present remain in the food. Control: buy raw materials from approved suppliers and test them on reception; observe withdrawal periods on farms; store chemicals separately using food-grade materials; keep traceability records with lot codes so that a batch can be recalled; official agencies sample and test food and act against premises that breach the regulations.
